name: Arkadi Monastery
scope: Surviving central double-aisle Katholikon and immediately enclosing monastic wings/gate, using each original building/roof plan; courtyard is open. Detached ossuary/memorial, restaurant, other detached station/service structures, landscape and interiors excluded.
era: Surviving monastery on current native building plans, with2008church facade and2015west-wing originals as exterior controls. No1866battle or vanished historical reconstruction.

originalReview.notes: Exact3072x2304native fully inspected: pale limestone double-aisle west front; two real doors and a central blind niche, paired lower oculi, columns/pilasters/cornices, scroll-edged twin gables with corner pinnacles, and the distinctive open2+1bell gable with central circular void. People, plants and signs excluded.

Exact4632x3464native fully inspected: north end of the west exterior wing, irregular warm rubble masonry with pale dressed window/door surrounds, sparse rectangular upper windows, lower arched doorways, parapet and bounded chimney/vent openings. No photographic texture, vegetation, poles or landscape copied.

review.method: Qualla-first corpus search followed by two exact Commons creator-released native originals and pinned primary revisions; native monastery/building plans inspected separately.
review.notes: Qualla-first search of63local candidates completed: modern photographs require attribution/share-alike; eligible CC0files are an unrelated street sign, Preveli monastery and Phaistos landscape. Battle/historic engravings do not control the surviving monastery and uncertain authorship/basis is excluded. Two exact additional originals from clearly named photographers are used: Klaas1978own-workPD-selfand Cmessierown-workCC0, each with pinned primary Commons revision, native image bytes/SHA1 and explicit creator release. Both originals fully inspected. No other imagery used.

Cat in Arkadi Monastery (Μονή Αρκαδίου), Amnatos, Crete, GreeceThe Arkadi Monastery on Crete, completed in its current Renaissance splendor in the 16th century, is the central symbol of the Cretan struggle for freedom. Its history is inextricably linked to November 9, 1866: during the Cretan uprising against Ottoman rule, nearly 1,000 people, mostly women and children, sought refuge behind the monastery walls.After a two-day siege by superior forces, Ottoman troops stormed the complex. To avoid captivity and shame, the defenders blew up the powder magazine themselves on the abbot’s orders. This self-sacrifice sparked horror and solidarity around the world and ultimately led to the independence of Crete. Today, Arkadi Monastery is a national shrine, whose ruins of the powder magazine and bullet-riddled iconostasis serve as memorials to the resistance.
